However, glycerol mixtures are still polar and readily miscible with water; their substitution for water-immiscible organic solvents is not plausible. Several hydrophobic natural terpenes and their derivatives (e.g., limonene, α-pinene, β-pinene, and p-cymene) are regarded as bio-based solvents to replace non-polar petroleum-based solvents (Boutekedjiret, Vian, & Chemat, 2014). Among them, limonene, which is a natural oil abundant in many renewable feedstocks such as citrus waste, has been studied the most. Recently, terpenes have been adopted in the prepa- ration of hydrophobic eutectic solvents, including menthol (Ribeiro, Florindo, Iff, Coelho, & Marrucho, 2015), thymol (Martins, Crespo, Pontes, Silva, Bulow, Maximo, et al., 2018), and limonene (Pereira, Silva, Rodrigues, Reis, Paiva, Duarte, et al., 2019). The resulting terpene-based DESs possess significantly reduced viscosity when compared to hydrophilic DESs, as Coulombic charge interactions are absent (Florindo, Branco, & Marrucho, 2019). These solvents have attracted increased attention and form one of the major classes of hy- drophobic DESs (Lee, Jung, & Park, 2019). The selection and design of diverse hydrophobic solvents from natural sources are still a focus of the industry, in order to widen the application scope of hydrophobic green solvents for green chemistry. In our continued efforts to broaden the pool of hydrophobic DESs from natural resources, a natural terpenoid, (R)-(-)-carvone (hereafter referred to carvone) was identified as a potential candidate. Carvone is a monoterpenoid that is a dominant constituent (60%–70 %, v/v) in the essential oil of spearmint (*Mentha spicata* L.) (de Carvalho & da Fonseca, 2006) with a low melting point (247.7 K) (Gallis, Bougrioua, Oonk, vanEkeren, & vanMiltenburg, 1996). It has various biological activities, such as antimicrobial, chemopreventive, and anti-tumor effects, with low allergenicity and toxicity (de Carvalho & da Fonseca, 2006). It has been commercially used as a fragrance for hygienic and cosmetic products and has been applied as a monomer feedstock for the synthesis of functional bio-renewable polyesters (de Carvalho & da Fonseca, 2006). Carvone can be obtained directly from spearmint oil and can be synthesized from (R)-(+)-limonene (Lange, 2015). Despite its various applications, carvone has never been studied as a solvent. In this study, carvone will be investigated as a bio-based solvent that might form a series of eutectic mixtures, with diverse compounds with different properties. In this context, carvone was mixed with three different classes of compounds (fatty acids, terpenes, and a benzoate ester) at various molar ratios, and the liquid window of the eutectic mixtures was identified from the solid-liquid equilibrium (SLE) phase diagrams. The physicochemical properties of the eutectic mixtures were characterized and compared with those of carvone. Their equilibrium properties, which were calculated using a thermodynamic model, Conductor-like Screening Model for Real Solvents (COSMO-RS) (Klamt, 2005), were used to place these mixtures among various classes of conventional organic solvents. After biodegradability assessment, the carvone mixtures were applied to the liquid-liquid partition of a model system, composed of a hydrophilic and a hydrophobic dye. Finally, their application to LLE in real samples was performed on a well-known red alga, laver, which is rich in a variety of functional components, including hydrophobic pigments, carotenoids and chlorophylls, and hydrophilic phycobiliproteins, phycocyanin (PC) and phycoerythrin (PE) (Pangestuti & Kim, 2011). ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials and preparation of carvone-based mixtures R-(-)-Carvone and its counterpart compounds in the formation of eutectic mixtures, including heptanoic acid, octanoic acid, nonanoic acid, decanoic acid, (+)-camphor, (±)-menthol, (-)-borneol, thymol, and phenyl salicylate (salol) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MI, USA). Hereafter, the stereochemistry of the compounds is not indicated. They were used as received, without further purification. Detailed information on these compounds is provided in Table 1. Other chemicals including hexane, chloroform, toluene, peptone from milk solids, hydrochloric acid (37%), Nile red, rhodamine 6G, and Brilliant blue FCF were also obtained from Sigma-Aldrich unless otherwise stated. Laver (Porphyra sp.) was purchased from a local market in South Korea. HPLC-grade water and methanol were obtained from J. T. Baker (Suwon, South Korea). A series of eutectic mixtures were prepared by mixing carvone with other compounds at various molar ratios (Table S1), including those listed in Table 2. The mixtures were heated at 60 °C until a clear liquid was obtained, then cooled to room temperature. ## 2.2. Thermodynamic modelling using COSMO-RS COSMO-RS calculations were conducted according to previous studies (Klamt, 2005). Predictive solutions were achieved through a combination of COSMOtherm with the Turbomole quantum chemistry suite (BIOVIA COSMOtherm, Release 2021; Dassault Systèmes, Leverkusen, Germany) at the density functional theory (DFT) functional B88-PW86 with a def-triple-z valence polarized basis (TZVP) level. The charge density σ was used for the thermodynamic calculation of the interaction energy, including misfit, hydrogen bonding, and van der Waals forces. Sigma-profile for compound i, pᵢ(σ), which is the probability of finding a surface segment with a charge density σ, is defined as $$p_i(\sigma) = \frac{A_i(\sigma)}{A_i} \quad (1)$$ where Aᵢ(σ) is the surface area with charge density σ. Sigma-profile of mixtures, pₛ(σ) was calculated as the sum of σ-profiles of components using the following equation: $$p_S(\sigma) = \sum_{i \in S} [x_i p_i(\sigma)] \quad (2)$$ where $x_i$ is the mole fraction of component $i$. Sigma-potential, $\mu_S(\sigma)$ is the chemical potential of a surface segment with $\sigma$ in solution $S$, and is a measure of the affinity of system $S$ to the surface of polarity $\sigma$. This was calculated using Eq. (3): $\mu_s(\sigma) = - \frac{RT}{a_{eff}} \ln \left[ \int p_s(\sigma') e^{\frac{a_{eff}}{RT} [\mu_s(\sigma') - E(\sigma,\sigma')]} d\sigma \right]$ (3) where E($\sigma$, $\sigma$') is the total interaction energy, that is, the sum of the misfit energy, hydrogen bonding, and van der Waals interactions of two adjacent screening charges, $\sigma$ and $\sigma$', while a$_{eff}$ is the effective contact area. In this way, the $\sigma$-profiles and $\sigma$-potentials of carvone and nine carvone-based mixtures were calculated. Moreover, 150 classical solvents that have been previously studied for solvent classification (Durand, Molinier, Kunz, & Aubry, 2011) were also calculated. The temperature was set to 25 °C for all calculations. ## 2.3. Machine learning for clustering and classification The original dataset for each solvent contained σ-potentials at charge densities from -0.030 e/Å² to 0.030 e/Å² with an interval of 0.001 (61 variables in total) and was scaled by root mean squares. Data scaling and analysis were performed using R (R Core Team 2020, R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria, https://www.R-project.org/). The APClust package was used for the clustering of the 150 classical solvents, using the affinity propagation (AP) algorithm. The AP algorithm took the similarity between solvents as input, with similarity being a negative Euclidean distance (Frey & Dueck, 2007). Preparation of carvone-based eutectic mixtures The main aim of this study was to use carvone as a bio-based solvent to prepare hydrophobic eutectic mixtures with diverse compounds. For this, several classes of naturally occurring compounds that are reportedly components of hydrophobic eutectic solvents were considered. In this study, medium-chain aliphatic fatty acids (C7 to C10) were selected as the model components because they are easy to handle in terms of melting temperature and have frequently been used in the formation of hydro- phobic eutectic solvents (Lee, Jung, & Park, 2019). The fatty acids selected were heptanoic acid (enanthic acid), octanoic acid (caprylic acid), nonanoic acid (pelargonic acid), and decanoic acid (capric acid). For the same reasons, camphor, menthol, borneol, and thymol, from which hydrophobic eutectic mixture formation has been reported (Martins et al., 2018), were selected, among a variety of naturally occurring monoterpenes. Although a synthetic chemical, salol (phenyl salicylate), which has many applications including polymer synthesis and pharmaceutical preparation, was also included because it often forms eutectic mixtures with several monoterpenes (Makoś, Słupek, & Gębicki, 2020). FT-IR and ¹H NMR analyses of carvone-based mixtures The ideal eutectic point for each mixture series was deduced from the ideal curves (Martins, Pinho, & Coutinho, 2019) and used to prepare the representative eutectic mixtures. They were CH (0.60), CO (0.80), CN (0.74), CD (0.89), CC (0.73), and CB (0.86). The numbers in parentheses indicate xcarvone at the ideal eutectic point. The CT and CS mixtures, presenting no eutectic temperatures at any mole fraction, were prepared arbitrarily at xcarvone = 0.5, yielding CT (0.50) and CS (0.50), respectively. These nine eutectic mixtures were characterized for their physicochemical properties in subsequent studies. The mixture constituents contained functional groups (carbonyl groups, carboxylic acids, and hydroxyl groups). These groups can form hydrogen bonding interactions, which can be recognized by FT-IR and ¹H NMR (Hansen, et al., 2021). Fig. S3 shows the FT-IR spectra of the individual components and their eutectic mixtures. The carbonyl groups in carvone, fatty acids, camphor, and salol were clearly detected in the range of 1600-1700 cm⁻¹. On the other hand, the hydroxyl groups in menthol, borneol, thymol, and salol were barely observed between 3200 and 3550 cm⁻¹, and the O-H vibration in the carboxylic acids was too broad to be identified in the fatty acids. The eutectic mixtures displayed no discernible changes in the wavenumbers or intensities. Thus, the intermolecular interactions between the constituents could not be inferred. The pure compounds and their eutectic mixtures were subjected to ¹H NMR analysis, and the spectra are shown in Fig. S4. The ¹H NMR spectra showed no new peaks in the eutectic mixtures, confirming that no chemical reaction occurred upon mixture formation (van Osch, Dietz, van Spronsen, Kroon, Gallucci, van Sint Annaland, et al., 2019). No hydroxyl proton peak was observed in pure menthol and borneol, presumably because of its fast exchange with the residual water of the dissolution solvent (CDCl₃). Similarly, pure fatty acids did not present carboxylic acid protons. The ¹H NMR spectra did not allow exploration of the hydrogen bonding interaction in most mixtures because the functional protons capable of hydrogen-bonding interactions were also invisible in the mixtures (van Osch, et al., 2019). Only thymol displayed the phenolic proton at 4.8 ppm, which was shifted to 5.8 ppm in CT (0.50). This downshift indicates the hydrogen bonding interaction between thymol (phenolic hydroxyl group) and carvone (carbonyl group) (Kang, Namgoong, Son, Kim, Jeong, Jin, et al., 2020). Further NMR measurements by ¹³C NMR and 2D NMR may help to elucidate these interactions. 3.4. Thermal stability, viscosity, density, polarity, and water contents of carvone and its mixtures In TGA, a function of temperature versus weight loss is used to determine the evaporation and sublimation points of solvents. The TGA curves of the nine carvone mixtures revealed the onset (*T*onset) and peak (*T*peak) temperatures, which are listed in Table S2. Carvone and most mixtures presented a single decay of mass loss, similar to previous re- ports (Martins et al., 2019). The only exception was CS (0.50), which showed a second plateau. This was similarly observed in several eutectic mixtures including menthol:lidocaine (2:1) (van Osch et al., 2019) and camphor:sobrerol (2.3:1) (Martins et al., 2019) which had interactions between two pure compounds leading to different evaporation tem- peratures. Many eutectic mixtures showed *T*onset and *T*peak values be- tween those of carvone and the counterpart compounds; CM (0.76), CB (0.86), and CT (0.50) presented higher *T*onset or *T*peak values than those of the parent compounds. The significantly higher *T*onset value of CT (0.50) than those of carvone and thymol is likely due to azeotrope for- mation (Martins et al., 2019), although vapor-liquid equilibrium data are needed for confirmation. Low viscosity is a desirable solvent property that facilitates easy handling and fast mass transfer during the extraction process. Many of the so-called green solvents, including ILs and DESs, have been criticized for their high viscosity. Hydrophobic eutectic solvents based on menthol and thymol have been reported to have significantly reduced viscosities as low as 11.2 mPa·s at room temperature, while tetraalkyl quaternary ammonium-based solvents were still highly viscous (228–1139 mPa·s) (Lee, Jung, & Park, 2019). As listed in Table 2, the viscosity of carvone was 4.38 mPa·s at 25 °C, and the viscosities of the eutectic mixtures ranged from 2.18 to 10.11 mPa·s. In fact, all the mixtures except for CT (0.50) and CB (0.86) had decreased viscosity compared to carvone. The very low viscosity of carvone and its mixtures could provide these bio-based solvents with great advantages, in order to serve as efficient, readily applicable solvents in industrial extraction processes. The density of carvone was measured at 0.9590 g cm⁻³, which is in good agreement with a previous study (Florido, Andrade, Capellini, Carvalho, Aracava, Koshima, et al., 2014). All tested mixtures, except for CS (0.50), were lighter than water (Table 2). Their densities ranged from 0.9429 to 0.9754 g cm⁻³ at room temperature. CS (0.50) was heavier than water, with a density of 1.0878 g cm⁻³. Solvent polarity can be characterized in terms of solvatochromic parameters. The multi-parameter scale of Kamlet-Taft (KT) and the ET(30) of Reichardt's dye are commonly used parameters. However, they could not be measured for carvone and the mixtures, because the innate UV absorbance of carvone interfered with that of KT probes, and because several fatty acids hampered accurate absorbance of Reichardt's dye due to their acidity. Instead, Nile red was used to measure ENR as previously performed (Jin, Jung, Li, Park, & Lee, 2020), and the results are listed in Table 2. In general, the polarity of both the fatty acid- and terpene-based mixtures slightly increased, compared to that of pure carvone (ENR = 52.95). The only exception was observed in CC (0.73), which exhibited the highest ENR (53.14) among the tested solvents. In contrast, CT (0.50) was found to be the most polar (ENR = 50.60). These results together suggest that the carvone-based eutectic mixtures could be tuned to possess different viscosities, densities, and polarities by varying the type of counterpart. Limited water solubility can support the hydrophobic character of a solvent, and likely its insignificant loss into water, when the solvent is used with water in LLE. Many terpene-based hydrophobic eutectic mixtures have reasonably low water content after saturation with water. For example, the water-saturated mixtures of thymol with camphor and with borneol contained water at 1.8 wt% and 2.4 wt%, respectively (Martins et al., 2019). On the other hand, fatty acid-based mixtures displayed a varying range of water contents depending on the counterparts; decanoic acid mixtures with tetraalkyl ammonium salts could range in 1.8–6.9 wt% of water (van Osch, Zubeir, van den Bruinhorst, Rocha, & Kroon, 2015), while those with lidocaine could be as high as 20.6 wt% (van Osch, et al., 2019). The water content in neat carvone was measured 0.08 wt%, and the eutectic mixtures before water saturation contained 0.07–0.48 wt% of water (Table 2). After saturation 6 K. Li et al. Classification of carvone and its mixtures as substitutes for conventional solvents The selection of solvents is a critical task in the extraction process, and is under current pressure towards green chemistry. Many physicochemical properties, in combination with multivariate statistical analyses, have been employed to appropriately classify numerous solvents. Although KT parameters are frequently used as a quantitative measure of solvent properties, they are not available for all solvents in the literature, and they cannot be measured for certain solvents, as was the case in this study. Hansen solubility parameters are often employed for the rational selection of solvents; however, the calculated values may differ depending on the methods (Sanchez-Camargo, Bueno, Parada-Alfonso, Cifuentes, & Ibanez, 2019). In this context, recent studies have adopted machine learning and deep learning algorithms to predict the physicochemical properties of solvents (Hansen, et al., 2021). Aubry et al. used a COSMO-RS model to calculate σ-potentials of 153 classical solvents and applied principal component analysis (PCA) for dimension reduction of datasets, along with k-means for clustering of the solvents (Durand, Molinier, Kunz, & Aubry, 2011). Their approach showed that non-empirical information derived solely from chemical structures could potentially be used to cluster solvents and help select replacement solvents (Moity, Durand, Benazzouz, Pierlot, Molinier, & Aubry, 2012). As such, we attempted to place the new solvents, carvone and its mixtures, among various classes of conventional solvents. All told, 61 variables for each of the 150 solvents were acquired; after data scaling, the datasets were directly applied to a clustering algorithm without dimension reduction. The AP algorithm was selected for clus- tering, which is based on message passing between data points (Frey & Dueck, 2007). This choice had its advantages, in that it requires no cluster numbers and provides representatives or exemplars of clusters. As shown in Fig. 3, the solvents were divided into 13 clusters (clusters I–XIII). The hierarchy of the clusters is displayed in a dendrogram, and the σ-potential of an exemplar solvent is shown by the orange dashed line among the other solvents in each cluster. The exemplars for clusters I to XIII are 2,2,4-trimethylpentane, benzene, cis-1,2 dichloroethene, methyl isobutyl ketone, butanenitrile, _p_-picoline, 1,2-propylene glycol, 2-butanol, _N_-methylformamide, 1-butanamine, 2,2,2-trifluroethanol, trifluoroacetic acid, and water. The assigned clusters are indicated for all the solvents in Table S3. The present study produced a slightly larger number of clusters than in the literature (10 clusters) (Durand, Molinier, Kunz, & Aubry, 2011). The difference is largely attributed to the different clustering results for the polar protic solvents (clusters X – XIII), which were distinctly clustered from the other solvents. In the second step, the 150 datasets with cluster labels as a training set were applied to SVMs, which have been widely used for classification and regression analysis and have shown to work effectively in high-dimensional dataset analysis. The obtained classification model was used to predict the clusters of carvone and its mixtures. As displayed in Fig. 3, carvone was classified as cluster IV; however, its mixtures could be placed in different clusters depending on the partnering components. CC (0.73), CM (0.76), and CS (0.5) were classified together with carvone in cluster IV, which is represented by methyl isobutyl ketone and contains ketone- and ether-based solvents. It is reasonable to regard cluster IV as analogous to the aprotic dipolar cluster (Durand, Molinier, Kunz, & Aubry, 2011; Moity, Durand, Benazzouz, Pierlot, Molinier, & Aubry, 2012). It is also reasonable to presume that carvone and the three carvone mixtures may substitute for the conventional organic solvents in cluster IV. All of the fatty acid mixtures were classified into cluster VIII, which largely consists of aliphatic mono-alcohols, as represented by 2-butanol. CB (0.86) was unexpectedly observed in cluster VIII. CT (0.50), which showed the highest solvatochromic polarity, was found in cluster VII. Cluster VII, represented by 1,2-propylene glycol, includes various polar protic solvents with mono- to polyalcohol groups. The classification results above show that our classification model built from the σ-potentials enables reasonable prediction of the solvent clusters of carvone and its mixtures. Moreover, the results imply that carvone may be tuned by preparing eutectic mixtures with diverse compounds to serve as green replacement solvents. 3.7. Biodegradability of carvone and its mixtures Biodegradability is an important aspect of solvents, in order to ensure greenness (Clarke, Tu, Levers, Bröhl, & Hallett, 2018). Despite a limited number of detailed assessments, the biodegradability of DESs has been assumed simply based on properties of nature-derived constituents. Moreover, most studies have focused on hydrophilic solvents. Carvone is known to be readily biodegradable in a closed bottle test (OECD301D), and most of its counterparts are reported to be biodegradable. Nonetheless, it is still important to examine whether the eutectic mixtures will be as biodegraded as their pure compounds are. Here, the biodegradability of all the mixtures was carefully examined using a previously described cultivation method (Kondo, Nishihara, Shimamoto, Watabe, & Fujii, 1988). The mixtures were monitored for 0–5 days by extraction of the remaining compounds and subsequent GC–MS analysis. The experimental conditions for the liquid-phase microextraction were optimized using a one-variable-at-a-time strategy, including the type of extraction solvents (hexane, chloroform, and toluene), ultrasonic irradiation time (0–5 min), and amount of sodium chloride (0–200 mg) in reference to literature (Chiu & Kuo, 2020; Lee, Jung, & Park, 2019) (data not shown). Each test species incubated with the autoclaved inoculum (no microbe) was used as the negative control, and neat carvone was used as the positive control. The remaining amounts of test species relative to day 0 are listed in Table S4. After five days of incubation, half of the carvone remained intact, while the degradation was found to involve reduction of carvone to dihydrocarvone (data not shown). In the case of the eutectic mixtures, most were degraded in similar pathways, but sometimes at different degradation speeds. Specifically, faster degradation was observed in CH (0.60) and CS (0.50), and slower degradation was observed in CB (0.86) and CT (0.50) (Table S4). Collectively, it is concluded that carvone and carvone mixtures are reasonably biodegradable, indicating that they are suitable as novel green solvents. 3.8. Applications of carvone and its mixtures to LLE Carvone and the eutectic mixtures were applied to aqueous solutions containing two model dyes, rhodamine 6G (red) and brilliant blue FCF (blue). Fig. 4a shows that all these solvents were capable of forming a distinct phase from water. The red hydrophobic dye could be preferentially partitioned into the organic phase, which resided on the top of the water, except for in CS (0.50), which is uniquely denser than water. Next, carvone and the mixtures were applied to the LLE of valuable compounds from a real sample, laver. Laver is a red macroalgae that is popularly consumed as a food source and contains a wide variety of compounds with different activities and properties. In this study, major functional pigments in laver, two hydrophilic phycobiliproteins PC and PE, and three hydrophobic pigments, carotenoids, chlorophyll a, and chlorophyll b, were targeted for extraction due to their distinct colors and high economic value. Fig. 4b and 4c show that the hydrophobic and hydrophilic pigments could be extracted into the organic and aqueous phases, respectively, with varying efficiencies. Carvone and the mixtures that were placed in cluster IV, along with CB (0.86) in cluster VIII, generally displayed similar extraction yields in both the organic and aqueous phases. CS (0.50) produced the highest yields of PC and PE and displayed a significantly lower water content, despite a very similar polarity to CM (0.76) and CB (0.86) (Table 2). CT (0.50), which had a significantly lower ENR value compared to the other terpene mixtures and was uniquely located with polar protic solvents in cluster VII, showed the lowest yields for the hydrophobic pigments. These observations imply that the solvent polarity and the mutual solubility between the solvents affect the extraction efficiencies for the two classes of pigments studied. The fatty acid mixtures, which were all placed in cluster VIII, showed different extraction results. These mixtures showed increasing extrac-tion yields, for both the hydrophobic and hydrophilic pigments, as the carbon chain of the fatty acid elongated, with the exception of CH (0.60). Results show that CH (0.60) extracted the largest amounts of carotenoids and chlorophyll _a_, while also leaving no PC or PE in the aqueous phase. These results are presumably associated with the solvent polarity of the organic phase and the acidity of the aqueous phase. Specifically, the extraction yields for the hydrophobic pigments increased as the solvent polarity decreased (Table 2), and the yields for the hydrophilic pigments increased with decreasing acidity (pH 3.14 in CH (0.60) to pH 3.43 in CN (0.89)). The solubility and stability of PC and PE, whose pI values are around 4.1 to 4.2, can be deteriorated by acid (Orta-Ramirez, Merrill, & Smith, 2000). Indeed, the purple aggregates that are indicative of PE and PC precipitates were the most evident in the case of CH (0.60) and less evident in the others (Fig. 4b). It is inferred that the fatty acids in the eutectic mixtures, especially heptanoic acid in CH (0.60), which exhibited the highest water content (3.8 wt% when saturated with water) was slightly dissolved in water to acidify the solution. The above application experiments suggest that carvone itself could serve as a hydrophobic bio-based solvent in LLE. Carvone can form eutectic mixtures with fatty acids, terpenes, and a benzoate ester. The carvone mixtures showed a wide liquid win- dow, with a low viscosity (2.61–10.11 mPa·s). Carvone and its mixtures were immiscible with water (0.6–3.8 wt% water after water saturation) and reasonably biodegradable. Their physicochemical properties, including density, polarity, and thermal stability, differed depending on 10 K. Li et al. Food Chemistry 374 (2022) 131630 the composition of the mixture. These results imply that the solvent properties may be tuned by changing the counterparts to carvone and the molar ratios between the components. Although hydrogen bonding interactions in the carvone mixtures could not be evidenced by FT-IR and ¹H NMR, they were thermodynamically supported in the σ-pro- files calculated by COSMO-RS. Application of the σ-potentials to AP and SVMs modeling suggests that neat carvone and the camphor and menthol mixtures may substitute for aprotic dipolar solvents with ke- tone or ether groups (cluster IV). In the same context, the fatty acid mixtures and the thymol mixture were suggested to be substitution solvents for aliphatic mono-alcohols (cluster VIII) and polar protic mono- to poly-alcohols (cluster VII), respectively. All of the solvents were effective in partitioning the hydrophobic model dye in LLE and presented varying efficiency and selectivity in the extraction of natural hydrophobic pigments from laver. Taken together, carvone is proposed here as a new bio-based source of hydrophobic designer solvents, through the formation of eutectic mixtures with various counterparts. The produced carvone mixtures can serve as low-viscosity, tunable solvents for liquid–liquid extractions involving water.
